title: Slope from Standard Form: Why the Minus Sign Is There

scenes.title: What is the slope of 6x − 3y = 9?
body: Slope is hidden until we isolate y.
scenes.narration: What is the slope of six x minus three y equals nine? You may remember a shortcut, but the useful question is why that shortcut works. Here’s the idea: slope is the coefficient of x when a line is written as y equals m x plus b. Standard form hides that coefficient, so we uncover it by solving for y.

scenes.title: Where −A/B comes from
scenes.substitution: The x-term moves across, creating the minus sign.
scenes.narration: Start with A x plus B y equals C. Subtract A x from both sides, giving B y equals negative A x plus C. Then divide every term by B. Now y equals negative A over B times x plus C over B. Notice why the slope is negative A over B: it comes directly from preserving equality while isolating y, not from a rule we invented to memorize.

scenes.title: The sign mistake students make
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. In six x minus three y equals nine, B is negative three, not positive three. The minus sign in the slope formula and the negative sign already attached to B both matter. So negative six divided by negative three is positive two.

scenes.title: Solve it and interpret it
scenes.narration: Let’s verify by doing the algebra instead of trusting the shortcut. Subtract six x: negative three y equals negative six x plus nine. Divide every term by negative three: y equals two x minus three. The coefficient of x is two, so the slope is two. That means every time x increases by one, y increases by two.

scenes.title: Check the slope on two points
scenes.narration: Quick check: when x is zero, y is negative three. When x is one, y is negative one. The rise is two and the run is one, so the slope is two. The big idea is that negative A over B is just the slope-intercept coefficient revealed by isolating y. Keep the sign of B exactly as written, and the shortcut becomes reliable instead of mysterious.
